note: Three 7th chords on one root (sevenths-up:5), each on a staff of only its four notes with the root and the note that moved ringed, then named by ear in the game, its answers named as its buttons show them. The guitar arpeggio necks became staffs, so the drill works for any instrument; the root is moves (any key), named as {{=key}} and the chords as chord tokens (Imaj7, I7, i7), with a {{?key}} line on what stays the same.

exercise.title: Three 7th chords on {{=key}}
exercise.why: The three chords share a root and each differs from the next by one note, so when you can hear which note moved, you can name the chord.

cells.text: {{chord:Imaj7}} has a major 7th, {{7}}, a half step under the root. Tap {{1}}, then {{7}}, on the staff below, then tap up the whole chord.

{{chord:I7}} lowers that one note to {{b7}}, a whole step under the root. Tap {{1}}, then {{b7}}, then the whole chord, and go back to the staff above to compare.
Listen for the top note: a half step under the octave, or a whole step.

{{chord:i7}} keeps {{b7}} and lowers the 3rd a half step, to {{b3}}. Tap {{1}}, {{b3}} and {{b7}}, then the whole chord.
Go between the three staffs. Practice until you can say which note moved before you look.
{{?key}}On another root the notes are new, and each chord still differs from the next by the same one note.

Press Start in the game below to hear a chord on a new root each time. Pick Major, Minor, Dominant 7, Major 7 or Minor 7: Dominant 7 is the chord written 7.
Practice until the name comes before you work it out.
